strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: reducing the aggregate cost of constructing large collections of neural scene representations.

The combination of scene-specific tri-plane features, a shared learned basis, and latent-space rendering is coherent and yields substantial reported savings over RGB tri-planes: 2.23 versus 16.02 minutes per additional scene and 0.48 versus 1.50 MB.
Experiments on two datasets show broadly comparable rendering quality to the tri-plane baseline. Component ablations support the usefulness of combining shared and scene-specific features.
The paper explicitly accounts for stage-1 overhead and provides training pseudocode, hyperparameters, and separate results for the two scene subsets.
weaknesses: The broader efficiency claim lacks quality-matched comparisons. In Table 4, Instant-NGP achieves 37.71 dB versus 31.20 dB for the proposed method while requiring only about 5% more total training time. TensoRF also achieves substantially higher quality. Quality–time–storage curves are needed to establish a competitive tradeoff.

Novelty and positioning are insufficiently established. The latent-space objectives and training pipeline closely follow IG-AE, while the main new representation is a shared linear basis concatenated with scene-specific features. Comparisons against existing cross-scene representation learning, learned initialization, and shared-decoder approaches are missing; independent scene fitting alone is an insufficient baseline.

Stage 2 updates the shared basis, renderer, and decoder using only S2, potentially changing the reconstructions of S1. Appendix B reports results for both subsets but does not clearly establish that S1 is evaluated using the final shared components after stage 2. Retaining separate component snapshots would also affect storage accounting. This ambiguity matters for the claim that the final system represents all scenes and can incorporate additional scenes.

Evaluation is narrow: two homogeneous, synthetic object datasets at 128×128 resolution, with quality measured on only 50 sampled scenes per dataset. There are no heterogeneous collections, real scenes, higher-resolution experiments, repeated runs, or uncertainty estimates to substantiate broader scalability and generality.

The resource comparison is incompletely specified. Table 4 does not identify its dataset or explain why its tri-plane and proposed-method PSNR values differ from Table 1. Baseline configurations, convergence criteria, and parallelization details are insufficient to audit the timing comparison. The reported memory metric measures stored representations rather than peak training memory.

The ablations omit sensitivity to the number of stage-1 scenes, shared bases, and micro/macro feature allocation. These directly determine the amortization and quality–storage tradeoffs. Most timing gains already arise in the latent-only ablation, so the incremental contribution of the proposed decomposition needs stronger characterization.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: amortizing the cost of constructing large collections of neural scene representations.

Combining shared macro tri-planes, scene-specific micro features, and latent-space rendering is technically plausible. Against RGB tri-planes, Table 2 reports substantial reductions in second-stage training time (16.02 to 2.23 minutes per scene) and representation storage (1.50 to 0.48 MB), with broadly comparable reconstruction metrics.

The experiments include two datasets, held-out views, component ablations, and explicit accounting for first-stage overhead. The algorithm and hyperparameter tables provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The broad efficiency claim is not supported by quality-matched comparisons. In Table 4, the proposed method is only about 5% faster than Instant-NGP while achieving 31.20 versus 37.71 dB PSNR; TensoRF reaches 40.38 dB. These results establish different operating points, not superior efficiency at comparable quality. Quality–time–storage curves and baseline configurations tuned to the proposed method's quality would be necessary.

The contribution beyond existing work is insufficiently established. The latent-space objectives and training pipeline explicitly build on IG-AE, while the main architectural addition is a learned shared basis combined with scene-specific features. Comparisons against existing cross-scene sharing, learned-initialization, and amortized reconstruction approaches are absent; independently fitting each baseline does not establish competitiveness for the proposed multi-scene setting.

Stage 2 updates the shared basis, renderer, and eventually decoder while optimizing only the second subset of scenes. These updates can change reconstructions of the first subset. Appendix B reports results for both stages, but does not clearly establish whether first-subset quality is measured again using the final shared components. Retention measurements and frozen-versus-updated shared-component ablations are needed, particularly for the claim that additional scenes can subsequently be added.

The evaluation is narrow relative to the stated scope: two object-centric datasets at 128×128 resolution, including front-facing faces, with quantitative comparisons on only 50 sampled scenes per dataset. There is no evidence for heterogeneous collections, real-world scenes, higher resolutions, or downstream usefulness as a representation dataset.

The scaling analysis largely extrapolates fixed per-scene costs rather than measuring behavior across dataset sizes. Sensitivity to the 500-scene first stage, number of basis planes, and micro/macro feature allocation is largely unexplored. Reported 'memory footprint' measures stored representations rather than peak training memory, leaving the practical memory requirements of joint training unclear.

Experimental reporting leaves important comparisons difficult to audit. Table 4 does not identify its evaluation dataset or explain why its PSNR values differ from Table 1, and baseline configurations and convergence criteria are insufficiently specified. Uncertainty estimates are also absent, which matters particularly for the small runtime advantage over Instant-NGP.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: reducing the aggregate cost of fitting scene representations across large datasets by sharing information between scenes.

The Micro-Macro decomposition is simple and technically plausible. Combining scene-specific features with a learned shared tri-plane basis provides a compact representation with controllable capacity.

Results show substantial savings against the RGB tri-plane baseline: stage-two training falls from 16.02 to 2.23 minutes per scene and storage from 1.50 to 0.48 MB, while maintaining broadly comparable novel-view synthesis metrics.

The ablations examine latent rendering, local features, shared features, and basis multiplicity. The paper also explicitly accounts for stage-one overhead and provides training pseudocode and hyperparameter tables.
weaknesses: The broader efficiency claim is not established at matched quality. In Table 4, the proposed method takes 5.22 thousand minutes versus 5.50 for Instant-NGP, but achieves only 31.20 dB versus 37.71 dB. This approximately 5% time saving accompanies a substantial quality deficit. Quality-versus-time and quality-versus-storage comparisons are needed before concluding that the method offers superior resource efficiency.

Novelty and positioning are insufficiently demonstrated. The latent-space training objectives and staged optimization substantially reuse IG-AE, leaving the shared linear basis plus scene-specific features as the main contribution. Comparisons focus on independently fitted scenes rather than strong methods that also exploit cross-scene sharing, learned initialization, or amortized reconstruction. The latent-only ablation is useful but does not fully resolve this comparison gap.

The evaluation is narrow for the claimed scope: two synthetic, category-specific datasets at 128 × 128 resolution, with quantitative quality comparisons on only 50 sampled scenes. There are no experiments on heterogeneous scenes, real captures, higher resolutions, or downstream dataset utility. Sensitivity to the number of stage-one scenes, basis size, and feature allocation is also largely unexplored.

Stage two updates the shared basis, renderer, and decoder using only the second subset while leaving the first subset's scene-specific parameters fixed. This can change the earlier scenes' reconstructions. Appendix B reports metrics for both subsets, but does not clearly establish whether first-subset quality is measured after all stage-two updates or quantify degradation. Preservation of previously learned scenes and the claim of supporting additional scenes need explicit validation.

Important reporting ambiguities weaken confidence in the comparisons. Table 4's PSNR values do not match either dataset's main results, and its evaluation dataset and aggregation are unspecified. Competing methods' configurations and convergence criteria are inadequately documented. Furthermore, the reported memory footprint measures stored model components rather than peak training memory, so it does not establish low working-memory requirements. These gaps, together with the missing competitive comparisons, leave the evidence below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reducing the cost of fitting and storing many planar 3D representations while retaining compatibility with image-based architectures. The combination of scene-specific features and a shared planar dictionary is simple and understandable.

The reported improvements over the implemented Tri-Planes baseline are substantial: Table 1 reduces second-stage training time from 64.32 to 8.96 minutes and marginal storage from 1.50 to 0.48 MB per scene, while improving average ShapeNet rendering metrics.

The evaluation includes several relevant representation families, component ablations, qualitative comparisons, and supplementary per-scene results. Reporting shared-model overhead and first-stage training costs in Table 6 is valuable, and the algorithm and hyperparameter tables provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The main quality comparison is too small to substantiate the broad claims about large scene collections: only four scenes per dataset, totaling 20 scenes, are evaluated despite fitting collections of 2,000 scenes. There are no confidence intervals or repeated sampling runs. The 50-scene supplementary experiments help, but cover only restricted comparisons on cars and faces rather than the full benchmark.

The incremental contribution over prior latent-space training is insufficiently established. The latent-space construction, losses, and two-stage fitting procedure are explicitly inherited from Anonymous (2025), whose reference contains no identifiable bibliographic information. Table 2 shows that latent training alone reduces time from 64.08 to 12.84 minutes, whereas adding the proposed shared planes reduces it further to 8.92 minutes. A stronger comparison against this underlying method and a smaller, storage-matched latent Tri-Planes baseline are needed to isolate the architectural advance.

The efficiency comparisons lack matched-quality or matched-budget curves and sufficiently detailed baseline training configurations. The methods operate at substantially different quality levels: Instant-NGP achieves 34.06 ShapeNet PSNR in 7.52 minutes, compared with 30.47 PSNR in 8.96 minutes for Fused-Planes. Thus, broad claims of outperforming essentially all non-SPARF methods in resource costs are not supported; the evidence establishes a more specific storage–quality–time trade-off.

The headline memory claims emphasize marginal storage rather than total collection storage. Although the appendix discloses overhead, ULW requires 384.19 MB of shared components: at 2,000 scenes its total is approximately 385.79 MB, versus 8.91 MB for CodeNeRF (MSIG). Consequently, 'lowest memory usage among all methods' is inaccurate for the demonstrated collection size. The reported memory metric also measures representation storage, not peak training memory.

Preservation of previously fitted scenes is unresolved. Algorithm 1 updates the shared bases, renderer, and decoder using only the second subset, although first-subset scenes depend on those same components. Tables 4–5 compare subset quality but do not specify whether first-subset results were recomputed using the final shared parameters or quantify before/after degradation. Retaining separate component snapshots would also affect the storage accounting.

The demonstrated scope is narrow: synthetic, category-specific objects at 128×128 resolution with dense posed views. There are no mixed-category, real-capture, higher-resolution, or downstream generation/reconstruction experiments. These omissions particularly limit claims that retaining planar structure provides practical benefits for the motivating applications, and scaling plots extrapolate fixed per-scene costs rather than establish quality and optimization behavior across collection sizes.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reducing the cost of fitting and storing large collections of planar 3D representations while retaining compatibility with image-based models.

The shared macro-plane dictionary combined with scene-specific micro planes is straightforward and technically plausible. Table 1 reports substantial improvements over the implemented Tri-Planes baseline: 8.96 versus 64.32 minutes per scene, 0.48 versus 1.50 MB of incremental storage, and improved average ShapeNet reconstruction metrics.

The experiments include several representation families, qualitative comparisons, component ablations, and supplementary implementation details. The explicit accounting for shared storage and first-stage training costs in Equations 11–12 and Table 6 is valuable.
weaknesses: The main comparative evaluation is too small to substantiate broad claims about large scene collections: only four scenes per dataset, totaling 16 ShapeNet objects and four faces, are evaluated across methods. No uncertainty estimates or repeated sampling are reported. The supplementary 50-scene experiments cover only selected comparisons and do not resolve this limitation.

The incremental contribution over prior latent-space training is insufficiently established. The autoencoder objectives and two-stage latent/RGB optimization are explicitly borrowed from Anonymous (2025), whose bibliography entry provides no title or usable identifying information. Table 2 shows that latent-only Tri-Planes already reduce training time from 64.08 to 12.84 minutes; adding the proposed decomposition reduces this to 8.92 minutes. The dictionary contributes useful compression, but much of the headline acceleration comes from the inherited pipeline.

The efficiency comparison lacks matched-quality or matched-budget experiments. In particular, there is no smaller Tri-Planes baseline matched to the proposed method's scene-specific parameter count, nor a systematic quality–time–storage sweep. Table 2 also changes the micro feature count from 10 to 32 when removing macro planes, so it does not cleanly establish the advantage over simpler capacity reduction.

The lowest-memory claim applies to marginal scene storage, not total collection storage. Table 6 reports 384.19 MB of shared overhead for ULW. At 2,000 scenes, its total is approximately 385.79 MB, versus 8.91 MB for CodeNeRF (MSIG). Although the appendix discloses these costs, the headline presentation overstates practical memory superiority. Storage footprint also does not establish peak training-memory efficiency.

Preservation of previously learned scenes is unclear. Algorithm 1 updates the shared bases, renderer, and decoder while training the second subset, without revisiting the first subset. Those updates can change first-subset reconstructions. Tables 4–5 report subset quality but do not clearly establish whether both subsets were evaluated using the same final shared parameters. Retaining separate checkpoints would instead affect the storage accounting.

The demonstrated scope is narrow: synthetic, object-centric data at 128×128 resolution. There is no validation on higher-resolution scenes, heterogeneous collections, or a downstream generation/reconstruction task demonstrating the claimed practical benefit of retaining planar structure. Sensitivity to dictionary size, the micro/macro allocation, and first-subset size is also largely unexplored.

Some conclusions are stronger than the results support. Instant-NGP is faster and substantially higher in ShapeNet PSNR than Fused-Planes, while SPARF-128 is roughly an order of magnitude faster with higher PSNR, albeit worse LPIPS. The larger Cars ablation shows only a 0.08 dB PSNR advantage over Tri-Planes and slightly worse SSIM/LPIPS. These findings support a particular storage–quality tradeoff, rather than broad resource superiority or consistently improved rendering quality.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: reducing the cost of fitting large collections of 3D representations while preserving a planar structure compatible with image models.
The micro/macro decomposition is simple and technically plausible. Shared basis planes capture common structure, while scene-specific planes preserve flexibility.

The reported improvements over Tri-Planes are substantial: approximately 7× faster second-stage fitting and 3× lower incremental storage, with better average ShapeNet reconstruction metrics in Table 1.

The experiments include several relevant representation families, qualitative comparisons, component ablations, and supplementary training details. Equations and Table 6 explicitly account for shared storage and first-stage training overhead.
weaknesses: The main comparative evaluation is too small to establish performance on large scene collections: only four scenes per dataset are evaluated, totaling 20 scenes, without uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. The 50-scene ablation and subset comparisons help, but do not establish the main rankings across datasets and baselines.

The efficiency comparisons lack quality-versus-time curves, matched-quality operating points, and sufficiently detailed baseline optimization settings. Several baselines achieve substantially higher reconstruction quality, so their longer training times do not directly establish inferior efficiency. SPARF-128 is approximately 11× faster than Fused-Planes and achieves higher PSNR, although Fused-Planes has better LPIPS and preserves planar structure.

The claimed ability to retain all learned scenes after second-stage training is insufficiently demonstrated. Algorithm 1 updates the shared basis planes, renderer, and decoder using only the second subset, potentially changing reconstructions of the first subset. Tables 4–5 compare subset quality but do not clearly establish whether first-subset metrics are measured after these shared parameters have been updated. Retention measurements or an explicit checkpoint/storage policy are needed.

The novel contribution is relatively narrow: the latent-space construction, losses, and staged fitting procedure are explicitly inherited from Anonymous (2025), leaving the shared linear basis plus scene-specific residual as the principal architectural contribution. That reference has no identifiable title or details in the bibliography. The paper needs clearer positioning and stronger evidence separating the benefits of the new decomposition from those of the inherited latent pipeline.

The headline resource results emphasize incremental costs. At 2,000 scenes, Table 6 implies approximately 1,321 MB total storage for Fused-Planes and 386 MB for ULW, versus approximately 8.9 MB for CodeNeRF (MSIG). Thus, ULW has the lowest marginal storage, not the lowest total storage at the evaluated scale. Likewise, second-stage fitting time excludes a substantial initial cost. The paper acknowledges these overheads, but its broad efficiency claims need tighter qualification.

All experiments use 128×128 synthetic object or face images. There is no higher-resolution evaluation, heterogeneous scene collection, or downstream generation/reconstruction experiment validating the central motivation of compatibility with image models. Sensitivity to the number of basis planes, micro/macro allocation, and first-subset size is also largely unexplored. These limitations leave the practical scope and scalability insufficiently established for acceptance.
